title: Meta stock sinks 6% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
content:
Meta shares slumped roughly 6% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.
The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans.
Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion to $145 billion.
Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.
The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."
Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.
Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.
Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable to the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for.
—CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

report.summary: Meta shares fell 6% after Q3 free cash flow turned negative and capex guidance rose, signaling investor anxiety over its aggressive AI spending.
report.background: Meta is in the middle of an expensive AI arms race, building data centers and buying chips to power ad-ranking models, AI assistants, and its Llama model family. Like other hyperscalers, it has ramped capital expenditures sharply, but Meta's spending is colliding with investor demands for clearer returns. The company's revenue is still growing fast, yet negative free cash flow shows how much cash the AI buildout is absorbing. The credit market reaction—five-year credit default swap spreads hitting all-time highs—suggests investors are starting to price in balance-sheet risk, not just growth. Meta also created a new Class C nonvoting stock to preserve founder control and give it more financing flexibility, while a California wealth-tax debate added a governance and political dimension to the quarter.
key_points: Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in Q3 and raised the low end of its full-year capex guidance to $135 billion, from $130 billion. The top end stays at $145 billion, so the company is signaling that AI infrastructure spending will remain heavy.

Revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.60 billion, beating analyst expectations of $63.37 billion. But earnings per share came in at $3.83, and the company said it was not clear whether that figure was directly comparable to Wall Street's $5.75 estimate.

Credit investors are getting nervous. The spread on Meta's five-year credit default swaps reached an all-time high, a market signal that investors see rising risk in the company's debt profile as it borrows and spends more on AI.

Meta unveiled a new Class C nonvoting common stock meant to maintain its “founder-led structure” and give it more ability to finance growth. The filing also said the plan helped convince CEO Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California amid a proposed wealth tax.

The stock fell about 6% as investors balanced strong revenue growth against negative free cash flow, higher capex, and governance changes. The reaction shows that AI spending is increasingly being judged on cash returns, not just top-line growth.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's results reinforce a new phase: investors still want growth, but they are scrutinizing the cash cost of AI infrastructure. Other hyperscalers may face similar pressure to justify capex with measurable revenue or efficiency gains. For developers, Meta's continued AI investment likely means more capable Llama models and AI features, but tighter budgets could affect how openly it releases future work. For regular users, the immediate impact is indirect: more AI features in Meta apps, but also more ads and monetization pressure as the company seeks to fund its buildout. Rising credit concerns could also make future AI borrowing more expensive across the sector.
